headline: Massachusetts hemp report sets out four models, backs none
dek: The Massachusetts Cannabis Control Commission's report to lawmakers offers four ways to regulate hemp THC, with draft rules only for licensed-store sales.
key_points: The Massachusetts Cannabis Control Commission's hemp report, approved unanimously on 17 November and due at the legislature by 15 December, lays out four regulatory models without choosing one.
Only Model 1, which would confine intoxicating hemp products to licensed marijuana retailers for adults 21 and over, comes with draft commission regulations attached.
The report keeps hemp cultivation with the Department of Agricultural Resources under every option and lists tax choices from sales tax alone to a potency-based excise.
Commission staff bring draft rules to the 10 December meeting, a day before the federal 0.4 mg total THC per container cap is due to take effect.
body: Massachusetts regulators have put four options for hemp-derived THC in front of the legislature and declined to rank them. The report the Cannabis Control Commission approved unanimously on 17 November, published in the commission's meeting packet, sets out models ranging from selling intoxicating hemp only in licensed cannabis stores to banning chemically converted products outright. The commission, it says, does not identify one model as a preferred comprehensive framework.

Coverage of the vote, including our own on 20 November, which relied on reporting by MJBizDaily and The Boston Globe, described the commission as seeking oversight of intoxicating hemp. The document itself is more cautious. It is a menu for lawmakers, though one option is far more developed than the rest: the report's Appendix D contains draft commission regulations for Model 1 alone.
## Why the report exists

Section 64 of Chapter 65 of the Acts of 2026, the state's latest cannabis law, told the commission to study how to regulate the hemp-derived cannabinoid market, working with the Department of Public Health, the Department of Agricultural Resources (MDAR), local boards of health, the Department of Revenue and the Alcoholic Beverages Control Commission. The law asked it to cover federal developments, licensing, testing, age limits, retail sales and tax, and to look at what other states have done. The finished report must be published and sent to the clerks of the House and Senate and to the Joint Committee on Cannabis Policy by 15 December 2026.

The draft is dated December 2026, with the draft regulations starting on page 41. It says products discussed are included because they are on sale, not because they are lawful; some are already banned or restricted.
## The four models

Model 1, a restricted age-controlled system, would allow intoxicating hemp products meant to be eaten or inhaled to be sold only by commission-licensed marijuana retailers, to customers 21 or older. Licensed product manufacturers would be the entry point for hemp ingredients, and products would face the commission's testing, tracking, packaging and labelling rules. The legislature would have to decide whether non-intoxicating hemp products must also enter that system. The report notes the model could squeeze existing hemp makers and shops that are not part of the licensed marijuana market.

Model 2 is risk-tiered. Rules and sales channels would depend on a product's intoxicating potential, dose, form or manufacturing method. Low-risk products could stay in general retail, while intoxicating ones would move to narrower, age-controlled outlets, possibly including licensed cannabis stores. Oversight could be split among MDAR, public health, the commission or another agency.

Model 3 keeps specified hemp products in general retail, including convenience stores and online, provided sellers and products are registered, tested, labelled and age-checked. The report warns this would mean overseeing far more retailers than either the commission or MDAR does now, and that such products would compete directly with marijuana retailers.

Model 4 would ban defined intoxicating, chemically converted, synthetic or semi-synthetic hemp products while allowing compliant non-intoxicating ones. The report records the Drug Policy Alliance's view that banning these products without a replacement framework may push some consumers to illicit markets, presenting it as a stakeholder view rather than a commission finding.
> Massachusetts has written the rulebook for one answer and left the question open: hemp THC belongs in cannabis stores, if lawmakers want it anywhere.
## What applies whatever lawmakers pick

Several recommendations cut across all four models. MDAR keeps hemp cultivation in every scenario; the report expressly does not propose moving the cultivation program away from it, because federal law requires hemp to be grown under an approved state, tribal or USDA plan. The other common threads are clear product definitions, finished-product testing scaled to risk, safeguards against youth access, rules for retail and online sales, separating intoxicating cannabinoid sales from alcohol-only retail, recall and civil enforcement powers, and enough funding and staff for whichever agencies are put in charge.

The alcohol regulator added its own points. If alcohol licensees are allowed to sell hemp-derived beverages, the ABCC recommended that the law expressly ban sales or delivery to anyone under 21, and noted that the state currently lets 18-year-olds handle alcohol at work.

On tax, the report lists the options without choosing: the general sales tax alone, a percentage-of-price excise, a potency-based tax, product-specific rates, or a wholesale excise such as a per-gallon tax on beverages. It notes a percentage excise is simple but does not track potency, while a potency tax would need standard testing that does not yet exist for hemp. If products moved into the licensed system under Model 1, lawmakers could amend the state's existing marijuana excise in chapter 64N of the General Laws to cover them.
## The federal clock

The report is landing just as the federal ground moves. The November 2025 funding law, Public Law 119-37, set a total THC standard for hemp and a limit of 0.4 milligrams of total THC per container for finished products. A later law, Public Law 119-103, pushed most of that change to 11 December 2026, the report says. Once the cap applies, most intoxicating hemp products on shelves today would fall outside the federal definition of hemp.

Congress could still change that. As we reported on 24 November, the White House has asked lawmakers to protect full-spectrum CBD products in the next spending bill. Other states are moving on their own timelines: as we reported on 23 November, Rhode Island has ordered hemp sellers to report their stock by 4 December.
## What to watch

Commission staff are due to present draft regulations at the 10 December meeting, The Boston Globe reported, one day before the federal cap is due. The final report goes to the legislature by 15 December, and the Joint Committee on Cannabis Policy would take up any bill in the 2027 session. Watch whether Congress alters the 11 December date in its December funding bill: a delay would give Massachusetts a live market to regulate, while the cap taking effect would leave the state choosing rules for products federal law no longer treats as hemp.
